groups.label: Sounds
groups.help: Which consonants and vowels exist, and how often each is used.

groups.label: Word shapes
groups.help: How syllables are put together and how long words tend to be.

groups.label: How words are built
groups.help: Whether grammar lives in endings, in little words, or both.

groups.label: Verbs
groups.help: Tense, aspect, mood, agreement and negation.

groups.label: Sentences
groups.help: Word order and how questions, copulas and pronouns work.

groups.label: Small grammar habits
groups.help: Little choices the grammar makes (each language settles them once).

groups.label: Word-making tendencies
groups.help: How the generator balances short, common, related and independent words.

settings.label: Language name
settings.help: Leave it on Random to keep the invented name.

settings.label: Consonants: fewer or more
settings.help: How many ordinary consonants the language has. Fewer gives a plainer, softer sound; more gives a richer one. The lowest allowed is the least that still lets the language make a unique, consistent vocabulary with your other settings. The generator picks which consonants. Complex consonants (below) are counted separately.

settings.label: Which consonants
settings.help: Choose the exact consonant sounds instead of just how many. Setting this overrides the count above.

settings.label: Complex consonants: how many
settings.help: Some languages treat a sequence such as ts, tl, kp or the Czech rzh as ONE consonant, separate from its parts. Pick none, one, a few or many. The generator chooses which ones; fix the exact list below if you want.

settings.label: Which complex consonants
settings.help: Each acts as a single consonant in syllables, has its own letter in the alphabet and its own share below, and never joins a consonant pair.

settings.label: How often each consonant is used
settings.help: Higher shares make a consonant turn up more in words.

settings.label: Consonant count when random
settings.help: How likely a small, medium or large consonant set is, when the count is left on Random.

settings.label: Vowels: fewer or more
settings.help: How many vowels the language has. The lowest allowed is the least that still gives a unique, consistent vocabulary with your other settings.

settings.label: Which vowels
settings.help: Choose the exact vowels instead of just how many. The five plain vowels (a e i o u) are easy to read; extra vowels are written with letter pairs. Overrides the count above.

settings.label: How often each vowel is used
settings.help: Higher shares make a vowel more common.

settings.label: Vowel count when random
settings.help: How likely each vowel count is, when the count is left on Random.

settings.label: Stress
settings.help: Which syllable of a word is said louder.

settings.label: Vowels side by side
settings.help: Whether two vowels may stand next to each other in one word (like the 'oe' in 'poet').

settings.label: Syllable complexity
settings.help: A starting point for syllable shapes: 1 is simple (ma-ni), 5 allows heavy clusters (strants).

settings.label: Syllable shapes and how common each is
settings.help: C is a consonant and V a vowel. CV is 'ma', CVC is 'man', CCV is 'pla'. Set a share to 0 to forbid a shape.

settings.label: Consonant pairs that may start a syllable
settings.help: Pairs like 'pl' or 'st' at the start of a syllable. Only used by shapes that start with CC.

settings.label: Consonants that may end a syllable
settings.help: Only used by shapes that end in a consonant (CVC).

settings.label: Consonant pairs that may end a syllable
settings.help: Pairs like 'nt' or 'lk' at the end of a syllable. Only used by shapes ending in CC.
settings.unused: No syllable shape that ends in two consonants has a share above 0 right now, so these pairs are not used. Raise CVCC or CCVCC under syllable shapes to use them.

settings.label: Consonant pairs that may join two syllables
settings.help: Where one syllable ends in a consonant and the next starts with one, as in the 'nk' of 'on-ko'. Only the pairs ticked here can meet inside a word. Untick everything for words with no clusters across syllables; tick them all for no limit.
settings.unused: No syllable shape that ends in two consonants has a share above 0 right now, so these pairs are not used. Raise CVCC or CCVCC under syllable shapes to use them.

settings.label: Longest run of consonants
settings.help: No word will have more consonants in a row than this.

settings.label: Typical root length (syllables)
settings.help: Average number of syllables in an ordinary word. Common words come out shorter, rare ones longer.

settings.label: Kind of language
settings.help: The overall style of the grammar. It also sets the defaults of many other settings that you leave on Random.

options.label: Isolating: short words with almost no endings
Agglutinative: endings stack on words, one meaning each
Fusional: endings blend several meanings together
Polysynthetic: long words that carry a whole sentence

odds.label: Isolating: short words with almost no endings
Agglutinative: endings stack on words, one meaning each
Fusional: endings blend several meanings together
Polysynthetic: long words that carry a whole sentence

settings.label: Endings per word
settings.help: Average number of meaningful pieces in a word. 1 is one piece (no endings); 5 is very long words.

settings.label: Where endings go
settings.help: Before the word, after it, or both.

settings.label: Number
settings.help: How many forms a noun has for counting.

settings.label: Who is the doer
settings.help: How subjects and objects are marked. English-like languages mark the object; ergative languages mark the doer of an action on an object.

settings.label: Cases
settings.help: Endings (or small words) that show a noun's job. The two basic cases for the chosen alignment are always kept.

settings.label: Genders
settings.help: Noun classes that adjectives and verbs may agree with.

settings.label: Plain form of paired words
settings.help: For pairs like king/queen, which one is the plain root and which is built from it.

options.label: The male word is the root
The female word is the root

odds.label: The male word is the root
The female word is the root

settings.label: Articles
settings.help: Words or endings like 'the' and 'a'.

settings.label: Counting base
settings.help: How numbers above the first few are built.

settings.label: Tenses
settings.help: Ways to place an action in time.

options.label: remote past, recent past, present, future

odds.label: remote past, recent past, present, future

settings.label: Aspects
settings.help: Whether an action is finished, ongoing, repeated, and so on.

settings.label: Moods
settings.help: Statements, commands, wishes, conditions.

settings.label: Verb agreement
settings.help: Whether the verb changes to match who does it (and to whom).

settings.label: Evidentials
settings.help: Verb endings that say how the speaker knows (saw it, heard it, guessed it).

settings.label: Negation
settings.help: How 'not' is said.

options.label: A small word before the verb
A small word after the verb
A small word on each side of the verb

odds.label: A small word before the verb
A small word after the verb
A small word on each side of the verb

settings.label: Sentence order
settings.help: The usual order of subject (S), verb (V) and object (O).

settings.label: Little place words
settings.help: Whether words like 'in' and 'to' come before or after the noun.

settings.label: Adjectives
settings.help: Where 'big' goes in 'big house'.

settings.label: Possession
settings.help: Where 'the king's' goes in 'the king's sword'.

settings.label: Relative clauses
settings.help: Where 'who sleeps' goes in 'the man who sleeps'.

settings.label: A word for 'to be'
settings.help: Whether the language has a dedicated 'is'.

settings.label: What the 'is' looks like
settings.help: A full verb, a small particle, or nothing at all.

options.label: Nothing (just put the words side by side)

odds.label: Nothing (just put the words side by side)

settings.label: Yes/no questions
settings.help: How a question is signalled.

settings.label: Dropping 'I', 'you'...
settings.help: Whether pronouns are left out when the verb already shows who.

settings.label: Question words go first
settings.help: Chance that who/what/where move to the front (only languages with verb-medial or verb-initial order).

settings.label: Plural after a number
settings.help: Chance that 'three dogs' keeps the plural ending (otherwise 'three dog').

settings.label: Order of big numbers
settings.help: Chance of twenty-three over three-and-twenty.

settings.label: Smallest small consonant set
settings.help: When a small consonant set is drawn, at least this many.

settings.label: Largest small consonant set
settings.help: ...and at most this many.

settings.label: Letter unevenness (low end)
settings.help: How lopsided the letter frequencies are: 0.3 is nearly even, 1.5 is very uneven.

settings.label: Letter unevenness (high end)
settings.help: Upper end of the same range.

settings.label: Fewest starting pairs
settings.help: When starting pairs are random, at least this many.

settings.label: Most starting pairs
settings.help: ...and at most this many.

settings.label: Fewest ending consonants
settings.help: When ending consonants are random, at least this many.

settings.label: Most ending consonants
settings.help: ...and at most this many.

settings.label: Common words are short
settings.help: How much shorter everyday words are than rare ones. 0 makes all words about equally long; 2 makes everyday words very short.

settings.label: Small words are short
settings.help: How much shorter little grammar words (the, of, and) are. 1 means no shortening; 0.5 makes them very short.

settings.label: Longest ordinary root
settings.help: No ordinary word starts out longer than this many syllables.

settings.label: Very short everyday words
settings.help: Multiplier on how many of the commonest English words get a one-syllable form. 0 turns it off.

settings.label: One- and two-letter words
settings.help: Chance an ordinary word may be a tiny one-or-two-letter word.

settings.label: Common words get their own roots
settings.help: Higher values make only the very commonest words independent roots; lower values give more rare words their own root too.

settings.label: Compounds become roots
settings.help: Chance that a word that could be a compound (like 'sunrise') becomes a simple root instead.

settings.label: Derived words become roots
settings.help: Multiplier on the chance that a word that could be built from another (like 'singer' from 'sing') becomes its own root.

settings.label: Families break up
settings.help: Chance that a related word leaves its word family and gets its own root.
